data.title: WebSocket
data.tagline: A connection that stays open, letting both sides send messages at any time
data.learningOutcome: In developer tools you can tell a persistent connection from a one-off request.
data.description: Live chat and collaborative editing may use WebSocket when both sides need frequent messages. An HTTP request and response form one message exchange, but the underlying HTTP connection can be reused and HTTP/2 can multiplex streams. After its handshake, WebSocket exchanges messages in both directions over one connection. Applications can add heartbeat checks and reconnection or state-recovery logic as needed; the connection can still drop.

learning.assumes: You have used chat rooms or real-time notifications, or heard of long connections.
learning.outcome: In developer tools you can tell a persistent connection from a one-off request.

distinctions.label: Ordinary HTTP request
distinctions.explanation: An HTTP request and response form one message exchange, but the underlying connection can be reused; after its handshake, WebSocket exchanges messages in both directions.

distinctions.label: Streaming response
distinctions.explanation: Streaming is one-way server push; a WebSocket is bidirectional, so the client can send anytime too.

explanation.title: Polling waits for the next check
explanation.text: A new message may wait for the next check; shorter intervals mean more requests.

explanation.title: WebSocket can send proactively
explanation.text: An open connection lets the server send proactively, but actual delay also depends on server work, queues, network, and client rendering.

explanation.title: Both sides can send
explanation.text: It is not just server push: the client can send anytime over the same connection.

data.boundary: A WebSocket does not guarantee the connection never drops: network switches and server restarts disconnect it, so auto-reconnect is needed. It fits real-time scenarios with frequent two-way traffic; ordinary page reads work fine with ordinary requests.

lessonPractice.title: A chat room is implemented by asking the server every second whether there are new messages. What problem does this cause?

options.label: Most per-second requests are empty polls, wasting requests and adding delay; real-time should use a persistent connection
options.feedback: Correct. High-frequency polling creates empty requests, and a new message waits for the next check; WebSocket can send proactively while connected, though processing and network delay still apply.

options.label: Checking every second is real-time enough, no problem
options.feedback: A message may wait nearly one polling interval for the next check, and most checks find nothing.

options.label: Make the page bigger so more messages show at once
options.feedback: Page capacity is unrelated to message arrival speed; the issue is how messages are fetched.

data.agentPrompt: The chat room currently polls for new messages every second. Switch to WebSocket: keep the connection open after it is established and push messages as they arrive. Auto-reconnect on disconnection; afterward confirm it is a persistent connection in the Network panel and test that messages resume after a network recovery.
